To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the sparse network topology is an efficient and reliable broadcasting structure; 2) the proposed algorithm is an efficient broadcasting algorithm; and 3) the proposed algorithm has high reliability.

(1) the number of links in a network is an important factor in the design of efficient broadcasting algorithms; (2) the degree of a network is a less important factor in the efficiency of broadcasting algorithms; (3) broadcasting in a network can be done in a time that is independent of the number of nodes in the network; and (4) a network can be designed so that the broadcasting algorithm is efficient, even if some of the links and nodes in the network fail.
(1) The proposed algorithm is the first to achieve a trade-off between the number of messages and the number of rounds in the case of unreliable links.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the broadcasting time of a network with maximum degree O(lgn) and with e-safe broadcasting algorithms is at most O(log n) for any n and e.
we show that sparse networks supporting efficient broadcasting exist.
the problem of broadcasting in networks of low maximum degree is very hard, but if one allows the use of sparse networks, it can be done efficiently.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the number of links in the broadcast tree can be significantly smaller than in previous works and that the number of transmissions can be reduced from O(n) to O(n log log n) by using a new type of broadcast trees.
broadcasting in sparse networks can be performed reliably in a time that is only logarithmic in the number of nodes.
sparse networks can have efficient broadcasting algorithms.
